analysis.one_liner: Requires private health plans to cover telehealth visits same as in-person care during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2020 with 10 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 public health emergency, this bill would have required private health insurance plans and employer health plans to cover doctor visits done by phone or video whenever the same visit would be covered in person. Plans had to charge patients the same copays and deductibles as in-person care, pay doctors the same amount as an in-person visit, and drop rules requiring patients to have an existing relationship with the provider. It applied only while the emergency period lasted.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private or employer insurance who needed care during the pandemic but could not safely or easily get to a doctor's office, including people seeking mental health or addiction treatment and people in rural areas. The bill says telehealth visits must be treated identically to in-person visits, so a video appointment could not carry extra cost or lower doctor payment than walking into a clinic [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover telehealth services whenever the same service would be covered in person, at the same cost-sharing (deductible, copayment, coinsurance) and the same provider reimbursement as an in-person visit [S2] [S3].

Bars plans from requiring a prior relationship with the provider and from restricting providers from delivering covered services by telehealth, opening remote access to new patients and to mental health and substance use disorder care [S3].
Lets plans waive cost-sharing for services diagnosing or treating COVID-19, including by telehealth, so testing and treatment would not carry out-of-pocket costs [S2] [S3].
Includes audio-only phone calls as a qualifying telehealth channel, which matters for patients without smartphones or reliable broadband [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private insurers and employers that sponsor health plans would bear the cost of the same-visit, same-price telehealth mandate while the emergency lasted, and any cost shift would land partly on premiums paid by enrollees and employers [S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring identical reimbursement for telehealth as in-person care, regardless of whether the remote visit takes less clinician time or involves fewer resources, would raise claims costs for plans and employers, some of which flows back to enrollees through premiums [S3].

Requiring coverage for telehealth even when the patient has no prior relationship with the provider, with medical necessity determined by the provider furnishing the service, invites heavier use of telehealth and makes plan oversight of appropriateness harder [S3].
The mandate is strictly temporary — it applies only during the COVID-19 emergency period — so it would not permanently fix telehealth access and cost-sharing rules that vary by state and plan [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — giving patients a safe way to see a doctor during a pandemic, at the same price as walking in — was real and timely, and it directly covered mental health care. Its main cost was forcing equal payment for remote visits that may be cheaper to deliver, which insurers and employers would absorb or pass through in premiums, and the temporary framing meant it would lapse rather than settle telehealth policy for good. On balance it was a modest, focused consumer-protection measure rather than a sweeping reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2020 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it; the bill died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the Health Care at Home Act of 2020 on May 14, 2020, joined by 10 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — its only action besides introduction [S5].
The committee held no markup or hearing on the bill and the full Senate never voted on it; no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans were spared the same-price telehealth mandate, and telehealth coverage remained a patchwork of plan-by-plan and state-by-state rules rather than a uniform federal requirement during the emergency.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employer plans dodged the mandate

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 14, 2020, requiring telehealth coverage parity during the COVID-19 emergency.

for.name: 10 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors (incl. Stabenow, Cardin, Casey, Udall, Shaheen, Harris, Klobuchar, Markey)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all from the Democratic caucus; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without committee action.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the Senate's 53 Republicans signed on; the Republican committee chair and floor leader took no action, so the bill had no Republican support and no Republican opposition vote — it simply never advanced.

industries.note: The bill forces plans to pay for telehealth visits at the same rates and with the same patient cost-sharing as in-person care during the emergency, including for new patients with no prior provider relationship. Insurers would absorb that mandate or pass it through to premiums.

industries.industry: Telehealth providers and telemedicine technology companies
industries.note: By guaranteeing payment parity and barring plan rules that restrict or penalize telehealth delivery, the bill guarantees a paying channel for remote care while the emergency lasts.
Mandated telehealth coverage, including audio-only phone visits, drives call, video, and internet traffic for doctor visits that plans must cover.
Group health plans are covered directly, so employers face added claims costs during the emergency; some may view expanded telehealth access as a net benefit to workforce health.
